text:
The storm howled relentlessly against the towering windows of the Astor mansion, a gaudy relic perched on the jagged cliffs overlooking the sea. Inside, the atmosphere was just as turbulent. Victor Astor, a wealthy but universally disliked art collector, had gathered his closest circle—or what could pass for it—in his study for drinks earlier that evening. Tension lingered in the air as the storm escalated, scattering the group to different corners of the sprawling house. When the clock struck midnight, a blood-curdling scream echoed through the halls, summoning everyone to Victor's private study. The sight that awaited them was ghastly: Victor lay slumped over his desk, his face frozen in a look of terror, an ornate scarlet scarf twisted tightly around his neck. The display case where the famed Crimson Serpent artifact had rested was smashed, its contents gone. Evelyn Astor, his grief-stricken wife, stood trembling in the doorway, clutching her silk robe as her cries cut through the sound of the rain pelting the windows.

###

Detective Charlotte Greer arrived at the mansion within the hour, her trench coat slick with rain and her sharp eyes scanning every detail of the disheveled scene. A seasoned investigator known for her cool demeanor and unerring instincts, she wasted no time summoning the four people who had been in the house at the time of the murder—Evelyn Astor, Lucas Kane, Mila Rivers, and Ned Hawthorne. As they gathered in the dimly lit parlor, their faces reflected varying shades of shock, fear, and something more difficult to pin down. Evelyn seemed the most shaken, her trembling hand clutching a glass of brandy offered by Ned, who hovered at her side like a concerned friend. Lucas stood apart, his broad frame tense and his jaw set as if preparing for an accusation. Mila fidgeted nervously on the edge of a chaise longue, her eyes darting between the detective and the floor. Ned, meanwhile, tried to break the silence with a nervous chuckle, murmuring something about how Victor had always lived dramatically, even in death. Detective Greer listened closely, her gaze lingering just a moment too long on Lucas, whose clenched fists and shadowed eyes betrayed a brewing storm of his own.

###

Detective Greer began her questioning with Evelyn, who hadn’t yet calmed despite Ned’s attempts to console her. “I don’t understand,” Evelyn stammered, her voice quivering. “Victor was… he was working late in his study. I was in my room most of the night. I only came down because I thought I heard someone shouting over the storm, and that’s when I found him…” Her words dissolved into quiet sobs, but Greer watched her carefully. Evelyn’s face was pale, streaked with smudged mascara, though her elegant composure felt slightly too rehearsed. “Did you see anyone else near the study?” Greer asked softly, her tone betraying no judgment. Evelyn hesitated for a split second before shaking her head. “No… no one. The house was so quiet it gave me chills.” Greer scribbled something in her notebook, considering the pristine silk sash of Evelyn’s robe, untouched by rain or grime, so unlike the storm-torn chaos outside the study. Evelyn clutched her brandy glass tighter, muttering, “Victor had so many people who hated him. But Lucas… he—” Her sentence trailed off as she glanced toward Lucas, her tearful eyes narrowing slightly. “He hated Victor most of all.”

###

Lucas Kane scoffed loudly at Evelyn's accusation, his fist slamming onto the armrest of the leather chair he was impatiently perched upon. “Oh, spare me the theatrics, Evelyn,” he growled, his voice dripping with derision. “Yes, I had my issues with Victor—who didn’t? The man was a conniving, selfish bastard who ruined lives without so much as blinking. But hate him enough to kill him? Don’t make me laugh.” His sharp laugh cut through the room like a dagger, though his eyes betrayed just the faintest flicker of unease. Greer took a step closer, fixing him with an even gaze. “You were heard arguing with Victor earlier this evening. I’m sure you don’t deny that?” she asked. Lucas folded his arms across his chest, his imposing frame leaning back as if to create some distance between himself and the question. “I won’t deny it,” he said coolly. “He owed me for what he did to me, my business, my future. He gambled with other people’s lives to make his fortune, and I wasn’t going to let him forget it. But I didn’t kill him, Detective. When I left the study, he was alive, counting his precious artifacts as usual.” His words were defiant, but in the flickering firelight, Greer noticed a small bead of sweat trickling down his temple. “Where did you go after that, Mr. Kane?” she pressed. Lucas hesitated, his jaw tightening. “Back to my room,” he said curtly. “Alone." The word lingered in the room, heavy with doubt.

###

Mila Rivers shifted uncomfortably as the attention turned to her, her hands tightly clasped in her lap. “I-I don’t know what else to say,” she stammered, her voice barely above a whisper. “I was organizing documents for Mr. Astor earlier in the evening—he had me come into his study to go over some contracts. But when I finished, I left. He seemed... preoccupied, like he didn’t even notice me leave.” Detective Greer leaned forward slightly, her pen poised over her notebook. “What time was that, Miss Rivers?” Mila furrowed her brow, clearly trying to remember. “It must have been just before eleven. I went straight back to my room after that. I—” She stopped abruptly, her face paling. “Actually, I did hear something,” she added hesitantly. “A crashing sound. I thought it was just the storm, but now... now I wonder if it was something more.” Her wide eyes darted toward the others. Lucas huffed derisively, while Evelyn avoided Mila’s gaze altogether. “And you didn’t think to investigate?” Greer asked sharply. “No—I mean, it wasn’t my place,” Mila replied quickly, her tone defensive. “I didn’t want to overstep. Mr. Astor hated when I meddled.” Greer studied her, noting the way her hands trembled slightly, but also the strange precision in her story. Mila seemed nervous, yes—but was it fear, or guilt?

###

Ned Hawthorne cleared his throat, breaking the silence that had fallen after Mila's testimony. “Well, now, if we’re all pointing fingers, I suppose it’s my turn to stand in the spotlight,” he said with a disarming grin, though there was something slippery about his overly casual demeanor. “Victor and I have known each other for years—far longer than anyone here. Sure, we had our spats, especially when it came to his collection. He wasn’t exactly... generous when it came to sharing the Crimson Serpent for exhibitions. We had words about it earlier tonight, but I’d hardly call it a motive for murder.” Ned’s eyes sparkled with an odd mixture of humor and defensiveness as he sipped leisurely from a glass of wine he must have poured himself. “Honestly, I was in the conservatory with a drink and my thoughts when all this awful business happened. The storm was so loud, I heard nothing until Evelyn screamed. A terrible sound, by the way. Gave me goosebumps.” Detective Greer studied his smug expression, her pencil tapping lightly on her notebook. Ned seemed unbothered, yet too at ease for someone in the middle of a murder investigation. “And where’s the Crimson Serpent now, Mr. Hawthorne?” Greer asked, her voice slicing through his attempted charm. Ned tilted his head thoughtfully. “If I knew, Detective, I’d probably be the dead one, not Victor.” His grin widened, but Greer noticed the faintest twitch in his left eye as he said it.

###

Detective Greer excused herself briefly and returned to the study, now sealed off as a crime scene. The storm continued to batter the mansion, its moans seeping through the walls, but Greer’s focus drowned out the noise. She crouched near the shattered display case that once held the Crimson Serpent. Glass shards littered the floor, though the jagged edges didn’t quite align with an impulsive robbery. Carefully, she ran her finger along the gouges on the wood beneath the shards. “Deliberate,” she murmured to herself. The drawer of Victor’s desk was ajar, and inside she found a slip of paper folded unevenly, as though it had been hastily shoved there. Unfolding it, she read scrawled handwriting: *“Midnight. You’ll get what you deserve.”* The note was unsigned and held no fingerprints, but its ominous tone sent a fresh ripple through Greer’s thoughts. Midnight—the exact time of Victor’s death. Was it a warning or a promise? She pocketed the note and then frowned at a trail of faint, muddy prints near the open window, leading toward the garden. With the storm, anyone would have been soaked to the bone, yet Evelyn’s silk sash and Lucas’s boots both bore no sign of mud or rain. Greer paused. Someone had either staged this or meticulously cleaned themselves up. Either way, it complicated the growing sense of deception.

###

Greer returned to the parlor, her gaze sharp as a knife as she rejoined the suspects. “The note found in Mr. Astor’s desk intrigues me,” she began, her voice calm but probing. “Midnight. You’ll get what you deserve. Anyone care to explain this?” Her question was met with a stunned silence, though a flicker of alarm crossed Lucas’s face for the briefest moment before he quickly masked it with a scowl. “Typical Victor,” Lucas muttered after a tense pause. “Always making enemies. That could’ve been left by anyone—clients, staff, creditors… He wasn’t exactly the type to inspire loyalty.” Mila shifted uneasily in her seat, her face pale. “Do you think it’s connected to the Crimson Serpent being stolen?” she asked nervously. Ned leaned back with a small smirk. “Theatrics—pure theatrics. Victor probably left the note there himself to make someone squirm. The man lived for petty drama,” he said dismissively, swirling his wine. Evelyn, however, remained silent, her hands gripping the armrest of her chair in a tension Greer didn’t miss. “Curious, isn’t it?” Greer mused aloud, her keen eyes flitting briefly to Evelyn. “A note like this doesn’t sound random. It sounds personal. Whoever wrote it wanted Victor to know something was coming.” She let the weight of her words linger, watching as Evelyn’s fingers tightened further, her knuckles whitening. Behind her feigned grief, was there something Evelyn wasn’t saying? Greer decided to push further, carefully baiting the tangled web.

###

Greer’s eyes settled on Evelyn, her voice lowering to a quiet edge. “Mrs. Astor, you seemed quick to suggest earlier that Lucas might have had the greatest reason to hate your husband. But I can’t help but wonder… did Victor ever provoke someone closer to him? Someone he trusted?” Evelyn’s head snapped up, her face filled with incredulous shock that bordered on offense. “How dare you?” she whispered, her voice shaking. “Victor was my husband. Whatever problems we had, I would never…” Her words faltered, and her hand went instinctively to her throat, trembling. Ned leaned forward protectively. “Come now, Detective,” he chimed in, his tone light but tinged with reproach. “Evelyn’s been through a terrible shock. She adored Victor, warts and all. Pouring suspicion on her is both cruel and absurd.” Greer raised an eyebrow, her focus unwavering. “Adored him, you say? From what I’ve heard, Mr. Astor’s marriage was more tempestuous than idyllic.” Evelyn shot to her feet, her thin façade of composure finally cracking. “You don’t know anything about our lives!” she exclaimed, her voice sharp and unsteady. “Victor wasn’t perfect, but neither is anyone in this room. If you want to find the killer, look at Lucas—he practically declared war on my husband tonight!” Greer stayed silent, allowing Evelyn’s outburst to echo in the dimly lit parlor. The widow’s words flared with righteous indignation, but beneath them, Greer sensed something more: fear. Whether for herself or for a truth she was hiding, Greer wasn’t yet sure.

###

Greer turned her attention back to Lucas, who was glaring stubbornly at Evelyn. “War, hmm?” the detective said, her tone neutral but probing. “Let’s revisit your earlier argument with Victor, Mr. Kane. You admitted there was bad blood. What exactly were you arguing about tonight?” Lucas met her gaze defiantly, his jaw tightening. “What does it matter now?” he snapped, though the anger in his voice felt more like deflection than outrage. “It was about money, as always. Victor owed me after he tanked my business with one of his schemes—but of course, he refused to admit it. He sat there smugly, drinking his fancy whiskey, telling me to stop whining and move on with my life.” Lucas leaned forward slightly, his voice lowering. “I told him if he didn’t reckon with the damage he’d done, it would catch up with him.” Greer raised an eyebrow. “And yet, he didn’t live long enough to reckon with it, did he?” Lucas scowled, clenching the arms of his chair. “For the last time, I didn’t kill him,” he said through gritted teeth. “After that argument, I stormed out. If you want to believe I came back and strangled him like some madman, be my guest, but you’re wasting your time.” Greer held his gaze for another moment, then glanced at the others. Lucas’s words were fiery, yet they rang hollow, as though he knew the closeness of his spat with Victor made him the perfect scapegoat. “We’ll see,” Greer replied coolly, her mind cataloging each element—his words, his rage, and the faint traces of nervous energy he couldn’t completely hide.

###

As the storm outside rattled the windows, Detective Greer turned her focus back to Mila, who had shrunk further into her seat, her hands trembling in her lap. “Miss Rivers,” Greer began, her voice firm yet measured, “you mentioned earlier that you heard a crashing sound near the time of Victor’s death. Yet you didn’t report it, even when you found out what happened. Why is that?” Mila swallowed hard, her eyes darting toward the floor. “I... I didn’t think it was relevant,” she stammered. “I mean, it sounded so far away, like it could’ve been something falling over in the storm.” Greer didn’t blink, the weight of her stare pressing down on Mila. “And yet, it happens to coincide not only with Victor’s time of death but with the burglary of the Crimson Serpent,” Greer pressed. “You were close to Victor—you saw and heard everything in that study. Were you aware of anything unusual leading up to tonight?” Mila’s body stiffened slightly at the question, her lips pressing into a tight line. She hesitated, her eyes flickering toward Evelyn, then back to Greer. “He was… distracted,” she said finally, her barely audible voice trembling. “Victor had been restless all day. He kept muttering about things being ‘out of hand,’ though he wouldn’t tell me what he meant. And I—” She broke off abruptly, shaking her head. Greer tilted her head, narrowing her eyes. “And you, what, Miss Rivers?” Mila’s lip quivered as she whispered, “Nothing. It’s nothing.” Her refusal to elaborate sent a ripple of suspicion through the room, Lucas glaring at her darkly while Ned observed her with a sharp, calculating curiosity. Evelyn, for her part, stared pointedly at the wall, her expression unreadable. For the second time that evening, Greer noted Mila’s nervousness and her darting gaze, as though she were hiding more than she dared let on. 

###

Detective Greer paced slowly across the room, letting the tension hang heavy as she gathered her thoughts. “It seems,” she began, her voice slicing through the silence, “every one of you had some form of conflict with Victor, whether over money, loyalty, or this mysterious artifact. But conflicts alone don’t commit murder. What I find most interesting,” she paused, fixing each of them with a pointed look, “is the small details none of you seem to notice about yourselves.” She turned sharply to Ned, catching him mid-smirk as he swirled his wine glass. “Take you, for instance, Mr. Hawthorne. You pride yourself on being a lover of art, yet you were very vocal earlier about wanting access to the Crimson Serpent. A priceless artifact conveniently missing now.” Ned raised an eyebrow, still leaning laxly in his seat. “Oh, Detective, surely you’re not suggesting I’d murder my dear friend Victor just to get my hands on a short-term treasure,” he said with a chuckle. “I’m a businessman. I deal in acquisitions above board these days. Killing just makes all… too complicated.” Greer didn’t flinch at his flippancy. “Would that explain why your boots, Mr. Hawthorne, were spotted wet by the servants earlier tonight? Despite the fact you claimed to have been in the dry conservatory.” Ned stiffened ever so slightly, the corner of his grin slipping before recovering. “Oh, you’ve caught me,” he drawled with mock sheepishness. “I had a stroll outside earlier for a bit of fresh air before the storm turned foul. Artistic inspiration—it helps.” Greer observed him silently for a moment, the faint crack in his smug exterior planting a seed of something bothersome. Ned was charming, no doubt, but charming men often made the cleverest deceivers. 

###

As Greer pondered Ned’s evasive response, a knock at the parlor door interrupted the simmering tension. A young constable entered, soaked to the bone from his trek around the estate grounds. He handed Greer a muddy handkerchief wrapped tightly around a small object. “Found this near the garden path, ma’am. It was partially buried in the mud,” he said grimly. Greer unwrapped the handkerchief carefully, revealing a miniature gold serpent charm—a fragment of the missing Crimson Serpent artifact. The charm’s ruby eyes gleamed even in the dim light, and the room collectively leaned forward in stunned silence. Greer tilted the charm in her gloved hand, her expression unreadable, then held it out for the group to see. “Interesting that this would end up outside, don’t you think?” she asked, scanning their faces. Evelyn gasped, clutching her chest as though the sight of the charm reopened a fresh wound. Mila leaned forward, her eyes wide with disbelief, while Ned gave an exaggerated shrug, his smile returning. Only Lucas seemed genuinely rattled, his hand curling into a fist on the armrest. “Anyone care to explain how a piece of Victor’s most prized possession just happened to wind up in the garden?” Greer asked, her tone calm but sharp. Lucas was the first to break the silence, his voice rough. “And you think this proves something, Detective? For all we know, someone planted it there to frame the rest of us.” Greer didn’t miss his accusatory glance toward Evelyn, nor the dark undertone in his words. She pocketed the charm, mulling over his remark as the storm roared louder, as if mirroring the mounting tension in the room. Someone in this house wasn’t just lying—they were toying with her, and she wasn’t about to let them win.

###

Greer turned her focus back to Evelyn, who had gone deathly pale at the sight of the serpent charm. “Mrs. Astor,” she said, her tone deliberate and precise, “your reaction is quite strong. Care to share what’s going through your mind?” Evelyn pressed her trembling fingers to her lips, glancing nervously toward Lucas before shaking her head. “It’s... it’s just shocking to see it,” she murmured, barely audible. “Victor treasured that piece more than anything. Knowing it was stolen—knowing it was touched by whoever did this—it’s horrifying.” Her voice quivered, and she blinked back tears, but Greer could see the tightening muscles in her neck, the clenching of her jaw. “You mentioned earlier that you were in your room all night,” Greer continued, her voice growing sharper, “yet you seem awfully knowledgeable about this being stolen, rather than simply… missing.” Evelyn flinched as though struck, her lips parting but no words escaping. Before she could respond, Lucas let out a bitter laugh. “Come off it, Evelyn,” he spat. “You’ve had your claws in Victor’s fortune for years. Don’t act like you’re just now mourning his ‘treasures.’” Evelyn whipped her head toward him, fire flashing in her tear-streaked eyes. “Don’t you dare lecture me about Victor’s money,” she snapped, her voice trembling with barely restrained fury. “You’ve been feeding off his wealth your whole life!” Greer watched the exchange closely, noting the way Evelyn’s hand gripped the pendant on her necklace—a glazed gold charm that seemed unnervingly similar in style to the Crimson Serpent. It was a subtle, almost unconscious movement, but it told Greer more than Evelyn realized.

###

Before Greer could press Evelyn further, Mila suddenly broke the silence, her voice trembling but louder than before. “I think you’re all ignoring something important,” she said, her wide eyes darting anxiously around the room. “Mr. Astor had been acting strange for weeks—paranoid, like he was expecting something terrible to happen. He even made me lock the study every night before I left, though he’d always unlock it himself later. The way he was acting… it’s like he knew someone wanted to hurt him.” The room went deadly quiet at Mila’s revelation, the faint crackling of the fire the only sound as they processed her words. “Strange behavior indeed,” Greer said thoughtfully, leaning forward. “And yet he trusted you to have access to his private space. That’s a great deal of trust for a man who was so consumed with paranoia.” Mila’s face flushed, and she shook her head quickly. “I only did what he asked—I didn’t question it. I didn’t want to lose my job!” she protested. Greer tapped her pen against her chin, her sharp eyes fixed on Mila. “And yet, you conveniently left out this particular detail earlier, even though it gives us more context for the state of mind of the victim.” Mila opened her mouth to reply but faltered, her face crumpling as tears welled up in her eyes. Evelyn looked away, her expression stony, while Lucas crossed his arms and muttered, “Convenient detail indeed.” Ned, meanwhile, was watching Mila with a curious gleam in his eye, as though filing her words away for his own reasons. Greer listened, but what she found most telling wasn’t Mila’s explanation—it was the palpable discomfort her revelation had cast over the entire room, as though some invisible thread had been plucked too hard.

###

Detective Greer stood, her movements slow and deliberate as she circled the room, letting the unease fester among the suspects. “If Mr. Astor truly believed someone was after him, then it raises a question,” she said, her voice smooth but cutting. “Who here would he have feared? Fear doesn’t come without familiarity—it comes from knowing someone’s capable of betrayal.” Her sharp gaze flicked to Ned, whose smirk faltered slightly under her scrutiny. “You, for example, Mr. Hawthorne. A friend of decades, yet with a history of shady dealings and a noted interest in the Crimson Serpent. Perhaps Victor worried old loyalties might crumble under greed?” Before Ned could respond, she turned abruptly to Lucas. “And you, Mr. Kane. Ruined by Victor’s financial ambitions, humiliated in public—certainly you had cause to make him fear you.” Lucas opened his mouth to object but stopped when Greer’s eyes narrowed. “But fear is rooted deeper than surface conflicts, isn’t it? Trust broken where it matters most.” She let her words hang as she finally turned to Evelyn, whose face remained frozen in a carefully composed mask, though her hand still reflexively fiddled with her necklace. “A man’s wife, his partner, would know his every weakness, every failing, every fear. If Victor couldn’t trust you, Mrs. Astor, who could he trust?” Evelyn flinched but quickly recovered, the spark of indignation returning to her eyes. “This is absurd,” she snapped, her voice trembling just enough to betray her nerves. “Victor may have had enemies, but I wasn’t one of them! I loved him, despite his flaws. He… he had secrets, Detective. None of us were privy to all of them.” Greer raised an eyebrow. “Secrets have a way of surfacing. Especially deadly ones.” Her words sliced through the room, and she noticed how Evelyn’s hand dropped suddenly from her necklace, as though caught in the act.

###

As the firelight flickered across the tense faces in the room, Greer made her way to the sideboard where a decanter of brandy sat, pouring herself a small glass as a deliberate, measured tactic. She turned back to face the group, taking a slow sip. “Secrets,” she repeated, her voice level but heavy with implication. “Victor’s death seems to revolve around one—or several. Mrs. Astor, you said earlier that Victor had enemies. You implied Lucas, naturally, but now you mention that your husband had his secrets. Care to elaborate on what you might have known?” Evelyn stiffened, her mouth parting as though to speak, but then she hesitated, her gaze dropping for a moment before she replied. “Victor didn’t tell me everything. He was... private, especially about his dealings,” she said quietly, her tone evasive. “He would disappear into his study for hours and refuse to let anyone disturb him. God knows what he was working on. And then there was the Crimson Serpent—he became obsessed with it recently, talking about selling it, even though he swore he never would. Selling it,” she repeated with bitterness, “was apparently his solution to every problem.” Greer leaned forward, her interest piqued. “Did you object to him selling it, Mrs. Astor?” Evelyn straightened suddenly, her poise snapping back into place. “What does that have to do with anything?” she said sharply, her defense too quick. Across the room, Lucas snorted disdainfully, watching Evelyn with narrowed eyes. “Hitting a nerve, are we, Evelyn?” he muttered. Greer put her glass down, studying Evelyn’s reaction closely. The remark about Victor selling the artifact seemed to have struck a crack in her armor, just wide enough for suspicion to seep through. “We’ll return to that,” Greer said calmly, filing the detail away. Secrets indeed, she thought, and Evelyn seemed to be holding onto one—tightly.

###

Greer didn’t let the tension dissipate before turning to Lucas with measured precision. “And what about you, Mr. Kane? You said Victor owed you—financially, I assume. But is that really what your argument was about tonight? Or was there something more personal in your grievance?” Lucas shot her a sharp glare, the veins in his temple visibly pulsing. “I’ve already told you everything,” he growled, his voice gruff. “Victor destroyed my business. He didn’t just ruin me financially; he humiliated me in the process. Do you know what it feels like to watch someone you once trusted gloat over your failure?” His tone crescendoed, anger flaring behind his words, but then, just as quickly, it ebbed and a flicker of restraint crossed his face. He exhaled sharply, leaning back in his chair, clearly aware of the weight of his outburst. “But I walked away after our fight tonight,” he added, forcing his voice steady. “I stormed upstairs—I didn’t even look back.” Greer tilted her head, unimpressed with his attempt at control. “You stormed upstairs, yet no one can corroborate your movements. You left Victor alive, you say, but you have no alibi. Convenient, Mr. Kane.” Lucas glared at her but said nothing, his fists clenching tighter. Greer let a beat of silence stretch between them. Then, finally, she asked coolly, “And tell me, Mr. Kane—if you didn’t kill Victor, how do you explain your well-worn boots leaving a trail of drying mud by the study window?” The room shifted, eyes darting to Lucas as his jaw visibly tensed. For one fleeting moment, there was a flash of panic in his gaze before it hardened once more. “You can theorize all you want, Detective,” he muttered, his voice low and dangerous. “But if I’d done it, I wouldn’t have left something as obvious as mud.” Greer studied him carefully. It was the tone of a man who resented being caught in a trap—but how much of that resentment was fear, and how much was truth?

###

The thunder outside crashed violently, punctuating the fraught silence that had fallen over the parlor. Greer turned her attention back to the serpent charm she had pocketed earlier, pulling it out and studying its intricate design one more time. “What strikes me as most curious,” she said, her voice breaking the stillness, “is how deliberately this charm was buried near the garden, almost as if someone wanted it to be found. But why hide something so significant, unless it was meant to mislead us?” Her statement hung in the air, weighted with insinuation. She looked between the suspects, their faces a mosaic of discomfort. Everyone seemed to be avoiding her gaze—except Ned. He leaned forward, his wry grin returning. “Perhaps because someone here wanted to stage a nice little drama for you, Detective,” he offered casually, gesturing with his wine glass. “Victor’s death made to look like a robbery, the precious Crimson Serpent conveniently vanishing, a trail of clues to keep everyone guessing. It’s all very theatrical, isn’t it?” Greer’s eyebrow arched as she met his amused gaze. “True, Mr. Hawthorne. It does reek of theatrics. But who here is clever enough, or desperate enough, to orchestrate it?” Ned sipped his wine slowly, giving a little shrug. “Certainly not me. I’m a lover of art, not chaos.” But there was an ease in his voice, a calculated charm, that set Greer on edge. “You do seem awfully unbothered for a man whose longtime friend was just murdered,” she said, her tone piercing. “Almost as though you’re enjoying the show.” Ned gave her a slow, deliberate smile, and for the first time, a flicker of unease crept across his face, almost imperceptible. Greer filed that moment away—Ned was playing a game, though the role he played was still uncertain. The question remained: was he playing mischief-maker, or something far more dangerous?

###

Greer’s gaze sharpened as she stepped closer to the fireplace, letting the tension smolder in the air. “Let’s revisit something Mila said earlier,” she began. The detective turned to the young assistant, whose wide eyes darted around nervously. “About Victor being restless, muttering about things ‘being out of hand.’ You said he didn’t explain himself, but you were the last person to work closely with him. You had access to his study, his documents, his collection. What exactly were you organizing for him? Maybe something tied to all of this?” Mila froze, her hands tightening in her lap. “I… I don’t know what he meant,” she stammered. “I was handling legal paperwork—a potential sale of some art pieces, nothing unusual. But he… he seemed different lately. Anxious.” Greer tilted her head, frowning. “A sale? Of the Crimson Serpent, perhaps?” Mila’s eyes widened. “No—I mean, maybe. I don’t know!” she said, spiraling into panic. “He didn’t tell me everything! He was private like that, even with me.” The desperation in her voice made Greer pause. This wasn’t the tightly controlled denial of someone trying to cover a crime; it was raw fear, as if Mila knew more than she wanted to admit but couldn’t bring herself to say it aloud. Evelyn, who had been listening intently, suddenly interjected. “Victor wouldn’t have sold that piece. The Crimson Serpent meant too much to him,” she said, her voice colder now, her words sharp as knives—but to Greer, Evelyn’s insistence held a strange edge, as though she was willing herself to believe it. Ned smirked at Evelyn’s outburst, clearly amused. Lucas just looked more irritated by the second. Greer glanced again at Mila, whose trembling hands betrayed her unease. There was a fracture in this group, widening by the second, and Mila seemed caught at its core. Greer wondered: Was she a victim of fear—or of guilt?

###

Greer’s eyes locked onto Evelyn as a sharp thought struck her. “Mrs. Astor,” she said, her voice cutting through the air like a knife, “let’s return to what you said earlier—that Victor’s solution to every problem was to sell the Crimson Serpent. Yet now you claim he wouldn’t part with it under any circumstances. Which is it?” Evelyn’s head snapped toward the detective, her face paling slightly as her perfectly constructed poise began to crack. “I… I mean,” she stuttered, scrambling for composure, “he talked about it, but I never thought he’d actually go through with it! He loved that piece—it was his prized possession.” Her voice wavered, but she took a deep breath and steadied herself. “When he brought up selling it a few weeks ago, I assumed it was just his way of venting about money troubles. Victor always exaggerated things when he was under stress.” 

“Stress,” Greer murmured, pacing slowly again. “The kind of stress that might involve debts, perhaps? Or something else Victor was keeping from all of you?” Evelyn stiffened but said nothing, her hand reflexively moving to her necklace again, fingers brushing against the pendant. Greer stopped in her tracks, her gaze zeroing in. “May I see that necklace you keep touching, Mrs. Astor?” she asked, her tone calm but firm. Evelyn’s hand dropped immediately, her face flushing. “It’s just a trinket,” she said quickly, almost too quickly. “Nothing of importance.” 

“Perhaps,” Greer replied, her sharp eyes narrowing. “But considering the Crimson Serpent itself is missing, any ‘trinket’ might be important. Humor me.” Evelyn hesitated for an agonizing moment, then slowly unclasped the necklace, reluctantly handing it to Greer. As the detective inspected it, the faintest flicker of recognition crossed her face. The necklace wasn’t just any trinket—it was remarkably similar in craftsmanship to the Crimson Serpent itself, down to the ruby embedded in its pendant. Greer’s lips pressed into a thin line. “Interesting design,” she said softly, watching Evelyn’s eyes dart nervously. “It seems Victor wasn’t the only one enamored with rare treasures.”

###

Evelyn’s breath hitched as Greer scrutinized the necklace, her fingers visibly twitching as though she wanted to snatch it back. “That’s all it is, Detective—a design!” she blurted out, her voice suddenly tense. “It was a gift from Victor years ago. A replica, nothing more. He… he had it made to compliment the Crimson Serpent. It’s not worth… it’s not…” Her voice trailed off as she realized she was rambling, and she quickly clamped her lips shut. Greer studied her for a long moment, letting the suffocating silence gnaw at Evelyn’s nerves. “A replica, is it?” she murmured, turning the necklace over in her hand. “How curious that you’d feel so protective over a simple replica while the man who gave it to you lies dead.” 

Lucas let out a dark laugh from across the room. “She’s full of it,” he muttered, shaking his head. “Victor never made replicas. He let everyone know when he had something valuable—wanted it to be one of a kind.” Evelyn’s glare snapped to Lucas, her polished facade fracturing into furious indignation. “And you would know so much about Victor’s habits, wouldn’t you, Lucas?” she hissed. “You’ve spent years bitterly watching him succeed where you failed!” 

“Enough,” Greer said sharply, her voice cutting through their spat. “Let’s set aside the replica theory for now and consider something else.” She held the necklace up, letting the ruby catch the flickering light. “The Crimson Serpent is missing, and yet here we have another piece of the same style. It seems Victor wasn’t the only one keeping secrets.” Evelyn’s anger fizzled into apprehension, her mouth opening slightly as Greer pressed on. “You know something about the Serpent’s disappearance, don’t you, Mrs. Astor?” Greer asked, her probing tone suffused with quiet authority. Evelyn tried to speak—tried to mount some form of defense—but instead her eyes dropped to the floor, her silence more damning than any accusation.

###

Greer let Evelyn’s silence stretch, the weight of it coiling tighter around the room like the storm pressing against the mansion’s walls. When Evelyn finally raised her eyes, they glistened, but it wasn’t grief that reflected there—it was something closer to fear. “Fine,” she said in a voice that was almost a whisper. “Victor planned to sell the Serpent... and he didn’t even have the decency to tell me. I found the documents in his desk weeks ago. He was cutting me out, stripping me bare. Not just the Serpent, but everything—our accounts, the house, even the few petty luxuries he permitted me. He said it was to pay off debts, but I knew the truth. He wanted to leave me with nothing.” Her trembling hand flew to her throat, where the necklace no longer hung. “I confronted him about it tonight. I told him he was selfish, cruel, that after all I had endured for him, he didn’t even have the dignity to consider me. He laughed at me!” Evelyn’s voice rose, anger leaking through the words like poison. “He said I was entitled. Said he owed me nothing.” She paused, her chest heaving as though the memory alone suffocated her. 

Lucas stared at her, his lips curling into a mix of disbelief and scorn. “So you killed him,” he spat bluntly. Evelyn whipped toward him, her tear-stricken face twisting with fury. “Don’t you dare,” she snapped. “He ruined your life long before mine. If anyone had reason to kill him, it was you!” 

Greer raised a hand, silencing the room once more. “Enough,” she said coldly, her voice cutting through the chaos. She stepped closer to Evelyn, her expression unreadable. “Mrs. Astor, you argue you had no reason to kill your husband—even as your own words betray your resentment. Did you confront him in his study tonight?” Evelyn’s lips trembled, her response faltering before it could take shape. Greer could see the walls she’d built around herself beginning to crumble.

###

The room felt like it was holding its breath as Evelyn lowered herself slowly back into her chair, her defiance melting into a brittle edge of despair. She pressed her hands to her face for a moment, her voice muffled as she finally admitted, “I did go to the study.” The words dropped like a bombshell, and everyone stiffened. “I went to confront him after I found out for certain he was going to sell the Crimson Serpent. I couldn’t take it anymore—everything, the lies, the years I wasted. But I swear, I didn’t kill him.” She looked up, her eyes bloodshot but burning with desperation. “Yes, I argued with him, screamed at him—but I left! He was alive when I walked out!” 

Greer crouched before her, her sharp, calm tone cutting into Evelyn’s unraveling confessional. “Alive, you say. Convenient, again, for someone whose story has shifted more than once tonight. You expect me to believe you had no hand in his death, even after admitting that everything drove you to that study—your resentment, your fear of losing the life he gave you?” Evelyn shook her head violently. “No, no, no! Someone else must have… I didn’t…” 

“Enough,” Greer said firmly, rising to her feet and pacing back toward the center of the room. She addressed everyone now, her voice carrying a quiet authority that demanded attention. “Here’s what I think happened. Someone here killed Victor, and someone here went to great lengths to stage this scene—breaking the case to imply a robbery, planting the charm outside to misdirect us, and letting suspicion bounce between each of you like chess pieces on a board.” Her eyes lingered on Lucas, Mila, Ned, and finally returned to Evelyn, whose panic had her twisting her fingers together. “The question is who among you has the cunning—or desperation—to pull it off, and who has the most to lose.” The storm raged harder outside, dark clouds swirling just as the threads of deceit did within the mansion.

###

Detective Greer stopped pacing, her posture straightening as clarity settled into her features. She turned back to Evelyn, her sharp gaze drilling into the widow’s now ashen face. “It was you, Mrs. Astor,” Greer said quietly but with absolute conviction. Evelyn froze, her breath hitching audibly. “You confronted Victor in the study tonight. You knew he was cutting you out, selling everything to leave you penniless. You couldn’t bear it—the betrayal, the humiliation. The Crimson Serpent wasn’t stolen, was it? You hid the piece yourself after you killed him, didn’t you?” Evelyn’s lips parted in horror, but no words came. Greer stepped closer, her voice calm but resolute. “You wrapped the scarf around his neck in a rage after he mocked you, after years of simmering resentment boiled over and spilled into something irreversible. And then you staged the scene to look like a robbery. The broken display case, the charm planted in the garden—it was all to deflect suspicion. You even tried to draw attention to Lucas, knowing his argument with Victor would make him the perfect scapegoat. But what gave you away, Mrs. Astor, was your carelessness.” 

Greer held up the necklace, its ruby catching the light one last time. “You handled this necklace as if your life depended on it. This is no replica, is it? It’s part of the Crimson Serpent itself—a piece removed by you long before tonight and kept as a contingency. And when the Serpent was eventually ‘missing,’ its absence furthered your story of a robbery.” The room fell utterly silent save for Evelyn’s shaky breathing. Then, at last, she broke, collapsing to her knees, tears streaming down her face. “He deserved it,” she sobbed, the final barrier of denial crumbling. “After everything he put me through—all the lies, the neglect… I couldn’t let him take everything! I couldn’t!” 

Lucas leaned back in his chair, his face unreadable. Mila stared at Evelyn in stunned disbelief, while Ned whistled low under his breath, muttering, “Well, I’ll be damned.” Greer simply nodded, a grim sense of satisfaction settling over her. “You can justify it to yourself all you like, Mrs. Astor, but betrayal is what ends people—even in death, Victor proved that.” With Evelyn’s confession, the pieces of the mystery clicked seamlessly into place. Outside, the storm began to wane, leaving the once-chaotic mansion in an eerie, vengeful calm.
